Issue No. 02 · October 2026

The landmark cases

Ten defining cases from 2023 to 2026, from brain implants to farm chatbots. Each record names the person, what changed for them, and where the account comes from.

Compiled 1 October 202610 cases
Area
Case 01 · USA
17
doctors seen over three years before an answer

A mother found her son's diagnosis

Courtney and her son Alex, aged 4 when symptoms began

Alex had chronic pain that no specialist could explain. His mother typed his MRI notes into ChatGPT line by line, including the detail that he refused to sit cross‑legged. It suggested tethered cord syndrome. She took that to a new neurosurgeon, who confirmed it on the scans: a hidden spina bifida with a tethered spine. Alex had corrective surgery and is recovering.

Read with care: the AI did not diagnose Alex. It gave a parent a lead that a specialist then confirmed. Doctors interviewed in coverage stress that chatbots are no substitute for medical care.
News TODAY interview, via Radiology Business ↗ How it was done →
Case 02 · USA
97%
of his intended words decoded correctly

A man with ALS spoke in his own voice again

Casey Harrell, 45, BrainGate clinical trial, UC Davis Health

ALS had left Casey understood only by his care partner, at about seven words a minute. Surgeons implanted sensors in the speech region of his brain in July 2023. AI models turn the signals into words, which are read aloud in a voice rebuilt from recordings made before his illness. By his second day he was using a 125,000‑word vocabulary.

"I have absolutely loved talking to my friends and family again."
Peer‑reviewed · NEJM Brown University ↗Reuters, via The Daily Star ↗ How it was done →
Case 03 · Switzerland
100 m
walked on a good day, after a decade of paralysis

A paralysed cyclist stood up and walked

Gert‑Jan Oskam, 40, Dutch engineer

A bike accident left Gert‑Jan unable to take a step. Researchers in Lausanne and Grenoble implanted one device over his brain and another on his spinal cord, and used an AI decoder to read his intention to move and pass it to the spine. He can now stand, walk and climb stairs, and has recovered some movement even with the device switched off.

"This simple pleasure represents a major change in my life," he said of standing at a bar with friends.
Peer‑reviewed · Nature CEA (French public research body) ↗ITV News ↗ How it was done →
Case 04 · England
16→48%
of stroke patients recovering with little or no disability

A retired postman walked again within weeks of a stroke

Shawn Theoff, 55, Canterbury, and stroke patients across England

When Shawn arrived at Kent and Canterbury Hospital, AI software read his brain scan in real time, helping doctors choose and start treatment fast. NHS England's early analysis links the tool with treatment starting more than an hour sooner, and with a tripling in patients who regain independence. It now runs in all 107 stroke centres in England.

Read with care: the NHS describes this as an association from early analysis, not a controlled trial.
Public health service NHS England ↗Digital Health ↗ How it was done →
Case 05 · Sweden
+29%
more cancers found, with no rise in false alarms

More women had breast cancer caught early

Over 105,000 women in Sweden's national screening programme (MASAI trial, Lund University)

Women were randomly assigned either standard double reading by radiologists or reading supported by AI. The AI group had 338 cancers found against 262, mostly small, early, node‑negative tumours. Full results in 2026 showed 12% fewer cancers turning up between screenings, the harder‑to‑treat kind, while radiologists' reading workload fell by 44%.

Peer‑reviewed · The Lancet PubMed record ↗ecancer (non‑profit) ↗ How it was done →
Case 06 · USA
0
people needed to tell her what she was wearing

A blind woman gained everyday independence

Chrichelle Brown, Washington, D.C., legally blind since birth

Using camera glasses linked to a free assistance app, Chrichelle asks an AI to read text, identify objects and describe what's around her. Without them she saw a reporter as a shadow; with them she could check her own outfit. She now teaches other blind people to use the glasses at Columbia Lighthouse for the Blind, and tells students the tool adds to the skills from their other classes rather than replacing them.

News NBC Washington ↗ How it was done →
Case 07 · Nigeria
6 wks
of tutoring ≈ 1.5–2 years of normal schooling

Teenagers in Benin City leapt ahead in English

Secondary students at nine public schools, Edo State

Students used a free AI chatbot as an English tutor in twelve 90‑minute after‑school sessions, with teachers guiding them. In a randomised evaluation they beat the comparison group in English, digital skills and AI knowledge, and also did better in end‑of‑term school exams. Each extra session attended added to the gains, and girls who started behind caught up the most. The authors estimate a 14% lift in future wages.

International development body World Bank working paper ↗BusinessDay Nigeria ↗ How it was done →
Case 08 · USA
+34%
issues resolved per hour by the newest, least‑skilled agents

New call‑centre workers got good, fast

5,172 customer‑support agents at a large US software firm

Economists from Stanford and MIT tracked agents as an AI assistant was rolled out to them in stages. Productivity rose about 14–15% on average, but the biggest gains went to beginners, who learned in weeks what used to take months. International agents' English improved, customers were more polite, and fewer asked for a manager. Staff were also more likely to stay. Top performers saw little benefit.

Peer‑reviewed · QJE NBER ↗ How it was done →
Case 09 · Kenya & India
1:1000
extension officers to farmers in Kenya; the gap AI is filling

Small farmers got an agronomist in their pocket

Sammy Selim, coffee farmer in Kericho, Kenya · Akula Sarswati, 38, two‑acre farmer in India

Sammy walks his slopes sending farm coordinates to a WhatsApp chatbot, which replies with a target yield and the exact fertiliser mix to reach it. Akula used a non‑profit chatbot, FarmerChat, to plan intercropping on her plot; over 225,000 farmers across India, Ethiopia, Kenya and Nigeria now use it. A survey of over 800 smallholders on similar tools found high satisfaction.

Read with care: farmers like these tools, but proof of higher yields is still being gathered. Randomised trials in Kenya are running through January 2027.
News · Non‑profit The Guardian, via NextBillion ↗ISDM case study ↗J‑PAL trial ↗ How it was done →
Case 10 · USA
<1%
of health‑coverage denials were ever appealed (KFF)

Patients started fighting back against insurance denials

Patients using free AI tools, including one built by the non‑profit Counterforce Health

Appeal letters are formal, technical and exhausting to write, which is why almost nobody files them. Patients are now using general chatbots, and a free AI assistant from a North Carolina non‑profit, to draft appeals and challenge large medical bills. Several states have meanwhile barred insurers from letting AI alone decide to deny care.

Read with care: patient advocates warn that people who aren't medical experts may not notice when an AI gets a medical fact wrong, which can sink an appeal.
Non‑profit news · Stateline Stateline, via Wisconsin Examiner ↗ How it was done →
